summary: Looks at problems with the prefix-length hint in DHCPv6 Prefix Delegation, where a client suggests the size of the prefix it wants. The original text is unclear about what clients and servers should do in various situations, so it summarizes the problems and gives guidance.

eli5.summary: A kid asks for a piece of cake of a certain size. This explains what the baker and kid should do when the size is not available.

questions: what is the dhcpv6 prefix length hint
how does a dhcpv6 server choose a prefix
can a client include a hint in renew or rebind
what happens when dhcpv6 cannot give the requested prefix length
subtitle: How DHCPv6 clients and servers should handle a client's hint about how big a delegated prefix it wants.

tldr.problem: DHCPv6 Prefix Delegation lets a client hint at the prefix length it wants, but RFC 3633 is unclear about what clients and servers should do when the hint cannot be met or when the client renews.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC walks through each message (Solicit, Advertise, Renew/Rebind), states the problem, and gives guidance such as sending the same IAID, using separate IAPREFIX options for a prefix and a hint, and falling back to the shorter, closest prefix.
tldr.outcome: A Proposed Standard that gives clients and servers a common way to treat the hint, while leaving servers free to ignore it by policy.

facts.label: Hint encoding
facts.value: IPv6 prefix field zero, prefix-length non-zero

today: RFC 8168 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2017, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 3633.

sections.title: Why the Prefix-Length Hint Needs Guidance
sections.content:
In DHCPv6 Prefix Delegation (RFC 3633), a client can send a prefix-length hint to say how big a prefix it would like. It does this by putting an IAPREFIX option inside an IA_PD option, with the IPv6 prefix field set to zero and the prefix-length field set to a non-zero value.

Servers are free to ignore the hint according to their policy. But some clients work badly, or only in a degraded state, with a prefix of a different length. For example, a client that asks for a /56 and gets a /64 might not be able to split the prefix across all its interfaces.

RFC 3633 is unclear about what each side should do in the various situations. This RFC summarizes the problems and gives guidance for clients and servers.
sections.eli5: When you ask for a certain size, it matters if you get a much smaller one. This document explains how to ask and how to answer.

sections.title: Building the Solicit Message
sections.content:
The RFC covers three things a client may want in a Solicit message, and each one uses the same IAID in the IA_PD. A new IAID is the surest way to get a completely new prefix, but that needs persistent storage on the client because a reboot would bring back the original IAID.

  • A prefix of a given length: the client MUST send the same IAID, put the length in the prefix-length field and set the IPv6 prefix field to zero.
  • The same prefix back: the client MUST send the same IAID, put the previously delegated prefix in the IPv6 prefix field and its length in the prefix-length field.
  • The same prefix, or else a given length: the client MUST send the same IAID, with the old prefix in one IAPREFIX option and the hint in another. The order of the two options does not matter.
sections.eli5: You can say 'a slice this big', 'the same slice as last time', or 'the same slice, but if it is gone, one this big'. You say which one you mean.

sections.title: How a Server Handles Solicit and Advertise
sections.content:
If a Solicit contains only a prefix-length hint, the server SHOULD first look in its prefix pool for a prefix whose length matches the hint, ignoring what it gave the client before. If there is no match, it SHOULD offer the prefix whose length is shorter and closest to the hint. The RFC's example is a request for a /54 where the server only has /30, /48 and /56.

If the Solicit names a specific prefix, the server SHOULD look for that prefix first. If it is unavailable and the client also included a hint in the same IA_PD, the server SHOULD then apply the hint in the same way. A server that will not assign any prefixes in a later Request MUST send an Advertise message as described in Section 11.2 of RFC 3633.

On the client side, if the Advertise offers prefixes the client can still use, the client SHOULD choose the shortest prefix length closest to its hint and keep asking for the preferred one in later messages. If the client sent only IA_PDs and cannot use the offered prefixes, it MUST ignore the Advertise messages and keep sending Solicit messages at the intervals set in RFC 7083. If it also asked for other stateful options such as IA_NAs, it SHOULD accept those and keep requesting the IA_PD prefix it wants, as specified in RFC 7550.
sections.eli5: If the baker has no slice of your size, the baker offers the closest bigger one. If you cannot use it, you keep asking politely, not nonstop.

sections.title: Renew and Rebind With a Hint
sections.content:
A client may accept a longer prefix than it hinted at (for example a /64 when it asked for a /60) but still prefer the original length. RFC 3633 is not completely clear on whether a hint may appear in Renew or Rebind messages.

This RFC says that when the client wants a length different from its current prefix, it SHOULD send Renew or Rebind with the same IA_PD and two IAPREFIX options: one with the currently delegated prefix and one with the prefix-length hint. This extends the lifetime of the current prefix, asks for the preferred one, and allows a graceful switch over. If the server cannot provide the new prefix but can extend the old one, the client SHOULD keep using the old prefix.
sections.eli5: You keep your current slice but ask again whether a bigger one is now free. If not, you simply keep what you have.

sections.title: How a Server Handles Renew and Rebind
sections.content:
A prefix that was unavailable during Solicit may become free later, for example after a configuration change or because another client stopped using it. Rather than making the server remember the original hint, the RFC says it is unnecessary for the server to do so, because the client's preference may have changed and the hint in the Renew message reflects what it wants at that time.

When the IA_PD carries both the delegated prefix and a hint, and the server assigned that prefix to the client, the server SHOULD do one of the following depending on its policy:

  1. Extend the lifetime of the original prefix.
  2. Extend the original prefix and assign a new prefix of the requested length.
  3. Give the original prefix 0 lifetimes and assign a new one. This avoids handling multiple prefixes but may break all the client's existing connections.
  4. Give the original prefix a 0 preferred-lifetime and a specific non-zero valid-lifetime, plus a new prefix, so old connections can finish.
  5. Leave the original prefix out of the Reply and assign a new one. The old prefix stays valid until its lifetime expires, which avoids sudden renumbering.

If the server does not know the client's bindings, for example a different server receiving a Rebind, it SHOULD ignore the original prefix and try to assign a new prefix of the requested length.
sections.eli5: When you ask again, the baker can let you keep the old slice, swap it, or give you both for a while so you can finish eating the first one.

sections.title: The General Recommendation
sections.content:
The overall advice is for a client that wants at least a prefix of a specific length to always include an IAPREFIX option containing just the prefix-length hint, in addition to any other IAPREFIX options for each IA_PD, in every Solicit, Request, Renew and Rebind message it sends.

A server is still free to ignore the hint. Servers that do honor it should try to assign a prefix of the hint length, or the next closest length that does not exceed the hint, if one is available. Whether a server favors the hint or avoiding a renumbering event is a matter of server policy.
sections.eli5: The simple rule is: always say what size you want, every time you ask. The baker may still say no, but at least knows.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content: This RFC adds guidance on client and server behavior and no new mechanisms. It points to Section 23 of RFC 3315 for security considerations in DHCP and to Section 15 of RFC 3633 for those of prefix delegation. It requires no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: Nothing new is added here, so the safety rules are the ones already written in the older documents.

viz.caption: WHAT THE CLIENT PUTS IN IAPREFIX (RFC 8168)

items.label: prefix zero, length set
items.desc: IPv6 prefix field is zero and prefix-length is non-zero: the client wants a prefix of this length.

items.label: prefix and length set
items.desc: The previously delegated prefix and its length: the client wants the same prefix back.

items.label: two IAPREFIX options
items.desc: One option with the old prefix and one with the hint, in any order.
